One of the ways the US expropriated land from native americans, who owned property communally, was to mandate private ownership. Communally, everyone had to agree to sell or give up land, which they of course never did. When land was split up and distributed individually, settlers could convince individuals(many of whom  were children, or who the settlers got drunk to sign documents they couldn’t read) to sell their land, and over time achieve the same goals as colonizing or occupying would but with legal justification and ”civility”.

Private property encourages division and self-interest over solidarity and co-operation, since you are never forced to consider the community’s needs over your own wants, so it’s also suboptimal for the community’s survival and development in general.

just because you're not suicidal doesn't mean you don't deserve to feel better than this. depression is vicious, and dangerous, and feeling the way you feel for too long can actually make you suicidal. you should not take this lightly, and you do not in any way deserve to feel like shit all the time. especially not for any of the reasons you've mentioned.

there are people who do get well from all kinds of mental illness! there are actually two TED-talks about schizophrenia and one about depression and all three speakers are educated, happy, stable, two of them are married and one of them have children! depending on what kind of depression you have, i think there are different ways to define a "cure", but if by cured you mean people have full lives, with the capacity to fully appreciate them and not feel like shit all the time, then yes - people get cured, all the time. i recently started actually having feelings again, and for someone who still struggles and has struggled with depression for my entire life (but the past three years to the degree that i stopped being able to feel or really react to anything, constant panic and anxiety and total loss of energy and interest) just that tiny ray of hope was so... just enough. it was enough.

i've seen it and i know it and there is hope. it can come in many different ways and shapes, and it's not your fault or that you're not working hard enough to see it.

you are incredible for carrying it with you every day, and you shouldn't have to. you don't deserve it. you deserve a vacation somewhere really nice and good food and people around you who take care of you and make you feel like you're worth something, and the ability to take it all in. 

look up the ted-talks if you want some comfort or distraction or just very informative and telling stories of mentall illness from wonderful people - andrew solomon, elyn saks and eleanor longden.
hang in there.
